content: Globally, approximately 38.2 million individuals are living with HIV as of 2013, according to UNAIDS. Despite the availability of various prevention strategies, such as condom use, male circumcision, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, and the use of clean needles, these measures have not been sufficient to halt the epidemic. In 2013 alone, 3 million new HIV infections were reported. This highlights the urgent need for additional safe and effective HIV prevention approaches. Men who have sex with men (MSM) bear a disproportionately high burden of HIV in most countries, even in regions with generalized HIV epidemics. Although there are effective HIV prevention interventions available for MSM, access to these services is often hindered by political and structural barriers, largely due to the stigmatized and marginalized status of this population. The high prevalence of HIV among MSM suggests that current prevention methods are inadequate, and additional prevention modalities are necessary. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) involves the use of antiretroviral drugs to prevent HIV acquisition in uninfected individuals. The concept of PrEP has been validated through laboratory studies in animals and real-world applications, such as the prevention of mother-to-child transmission and post-exposure prophylaxis. The safety of the drugs considered for PrEP, specifically tenofovir and emtricitabine, has been established through their use in treatment and safety trials involving uninfected individuals. Over the past decade, five clinical trials (Phase IIb and Phase III) have been conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of PrEP among various populations, including people who inject drugs, serodiscordant couples, heterosexual women, and high-risk MSM. One of these trials, the iPrEx study, specifically examined the efficacy of a daily combination of tenofovir and emtricitabine in preventing HIV infection among MSM. Conducted across six countries on four continents, the iPrEx study demonstrated a 44% reduction in HIV transmission in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. Adherence to the recommended regimen was a critical factor, with efficacy reaching 73% among men who reported taking the pills on 90% or more of days. Resistance to the drugs was rare and observed only in two participants who had undetected acute HIV infection at baseline. Safety concerns were minimal, and a trend toward risk reduction, including increased condom use and fewer sexual partners, was reported across all study sites. In 2012, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued guidelines recommending PrEP for serodiscordant couples, MSM, and transgender individuals at high risk of HIV. This systematic review updates the evidence on PrEP for MSM to inform the WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations. The updated review focuses exclusively on MSM and includes all oral PrEP regimens containing tenofovir, expanding beyond the specific combination of emtricitabine and tenofovir used in the iPrEx study. A review of MSM values and preferences regarding PrEP was conducted in 2011, based on data collected before the iPrEx trial results were available. However, awareness of PrEP's partial effectiveness may have influenced these values and preferences since then. The updated review includes studies published through the end of 2013, focusing on data collected after the release of the iPrEx results. The systematic review employed a comprehensive search strategy, including electronic databases (PubMed, CINAHL, and EMBASE), conference abstracts, and expert consultations. Articles were screened and assessed for eligibility based on predefined criteria, including randomized controlled trials evaluating oral PrEP containing tenofovir among MSM and measuring key outcomes such as HIV infection, adverse events, condom use, and the number of sexual partners. Ultimately, four studies reported in five articles met the inclusion criteria. These included one Phase III efficacy trial and three smaller pilot feasibility or extended safety studies. The primary Phase III trial, conducted among 2,499 participants in six countries, demonstrated a 44% reduction in HIV risk with daily oral PrEP. Adverse events were comparable between the intervention and control groups, and no significant differences in grade 3 or 4 adverse events were observed. Adherence to the regimen was a key determinant of efficacy, with higher adherence associated with greater risk reduction. The findings underscore the importance of PrEP as a prevention strategy for MSM, particularly when adherence is high. The WHO guidelines and systematic review aim to provide evidence-based recommendations to optimize HIV prevention efforts among key populations.
